bull.argument: Meta's 2025 results show strong scale and profitability. Total revenue rose 22% to $200.97 billion, and income from operations grew 20% to $83.28 billion. Growth was driven by both volume and price: ad impressions rose 12% and average price per ad rose 9%. Family daily active people reached 3.58 billion, up 7% year-over-year, and the company generated $72.22 billion in capital expenditures while still returning $26.26 billion through share repurchases and $5.32 billion in dividends. Cash and marketable securities stood at $81.59 billion. The filing acknowledges real headwinds, including privacy-driven limits on ad targeting, Apple iOS changes, and Reels monetizing at a lower rate. Yet the numbers show the core advertising engine absorbing those pressures: revenue grew across every user geography, and management reports that its AI-driven ad improvements are already producing better advertiser results. The company's heavy spending on AI infrastructure and Reality Labs is large, but Family of Apps still earned a 52% operating margin, which funds those bets.

claims.claim: Full-year 2025 revenue grew 22% to $200.97 billion, with operating income up 20%.
claims.quote: Total revenue for 2025 was $200.97 billion, an increase of 22% compared to 2024, due to an increase in advertising revenue.

claims.claim: Growth came from both more ad impressions and higher pricing per ad.
claims.quote: Ad impressions delivered across our Family of Apps in 2025 increased 12% year-over-year, and our average price per ad increased 9% year-over-year.

claims.claim: Management reports its AI-driven ad improvements are already producing results for advertisers.
claims.quote: We believe our ongoing improvements to ad targeting and measurement are continuing to drive improved results for advertisers.

bear.argument: Meta's headline growth masks a business that depends on conditions it does not control. The filing states that substantially all revenue comes from advertising on Facebook and Instagram, and that marketers 'do not have long-term advertising commitments' with the company, so budgets can be cut quickly. Management also concedes that privacy changes and Apple's iOS changes 'reduce our and other iOS developers' ability to target and measure advertising,' and that these developments 'will continue to adversely impact our advertising revenue for the foreseeable future.' The 12% rise in ad impressions and 9% rise in price per ad are real, but the filing says Reels 'monetizes at a lower rate' and is growing, which dilutes future monetization. Costs are rising fast: total costs and expenses grew 24%, and capital expenditures reached $72.22 billion. Reality Labs lost $19.19 billion from operations, and management expects 2026 losses 'to remain similar,' with returns possibly 'in the next decade.' Investors are being asked to fund very large, uncertain bets while the core engine faces structural pressure and a dual class structure limits their influence over these decisions.

claims.claim: Advertising revenue is highly concentrated and marketers can reduce spend at any time, since there are no long-term commitments.
claims.quote: our marketers do not have long-term advertising commitments with us

claims.claim: Management expects privacy and platform changes to keep weighing on advertising revenue for years.
claims.quote: the legislative, regulatory and platform developments described above will continue to adversely impact our advertising revenue for the foreseeable future

claims.claim: Reality Labs losses are large and expected to persist, with returns possibly far off.
claims.quote: we expect our 2026 RL operating losses to remain similar to 2025

bull.argument: The bear case concedes the core facts: 2025 revenue grew 22%, income from operations rose 20% to $83.28 billion, and Family of Apps earned a 52% operating margin. Headwinds are real, and the filing discloses them plainly. But the disclosed pressures are being absorbed, not overwhelming the business. Revenue grew in every user geography, including 21% in United States & Canada and 24% in Europe, despite the iOS and privacy changes the opponent cites. Pricing rose 9% even as targeting tools were constrained, which argues that advertiser demand remains strong. On costs, the 24% rise is explained by employee compensation and infrastructure, and Family of Apps still converted most of its revenue into operating income. Reality Labs' $19.19 billion loss is large, but it is a disclosed, bounded choice that the filing says depends on profits from other areas, and those profits are growing. The dual class point is real, but it is a governance feature investors can weigh alongside a company that returned $26.26 billion in buybacks and $5.32 billion in dividends while holding $81.59 billion in cash and securities. The question is whether growth in impressions and price keeps outrunning these pressures, and 2025 shows it has.

claims.claim: Revenue grew in every user geography in 2025.
claims.quote: In 2025, revenue increased by 21% in United States & Canada, 24% in Europe, 20% in Asia-Pacific, and 27% in Rest of World, in each case relative to 2024.

claims.claim: Family of Apps still earned a 52% operating margin despite rising costs.
The company returned substantial capital to shareholders and held large cash reserves.
claims.quote: Share repurchases of our Class A common stock were $26.26 billion and total dividend and dividend equivalent payments were $5.32 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025.

bear.argument: The opponent's case rests on averages that hide concentration and direction. Revenue growth is real, but the filing ties it to a narrow base: 'Substantially all of our revenue is currently generated from marketers advertising on Facebook and Instagram,' and those marketers can cut budgets without notice. Regional growth looks broad, yet the filing says ad impression growth is 'primarily in geographies that monetize at lower rates, such as Asia-Pacific,' so volume is shifting toward cheaper markets. The 9% price increase is also not free of risk: management admits it cannot 'quantify the exact impact that each trend had on our advertising revenue,' so the company cannot show how much of growth is durable. On costs, the filing says income from operations grew 20% while costs rose 24%, and it expects 'our AI initiatives will require significantly increased investment in infrastructure.' Margin is shrinking as spending climbs. Reality Labs is not a bounded choice: management says its profits are needed to support it and that returns may come 'in the next decade.' Buybacks and cash do not change that dependence on a single revenue stream.

claims.claim: Management admits it cannot precisely attribute advertising revenue trends, weakening confidence that pricing gains will persist.
claims.quote: we are unable to quantify the exact impact that each trend had on our advertising revenue during the periods presented

claims.claim: Impression growth is concentrated in lower-monetizing regions, diluting revenue per user.
claims.quote: ad impression growth is primarily in geographies that monetize at lower rates, such as Asia-Pacific

claims.claim: Management expects AI initiatives to require significantly increased infrastructure investment, raising future cost pressure.
claims.quote: we expect our AI initiatives will require significantly increased investment in infrastructure

judge.reasoning: Both sides cite verified quotes from the filing and make reasonable arguments. The bull's strongest point is that revenue grew in every geography and that pricing rose 9%, showing demand absorbing headwinds, while the bear's strongest points are the admitted inability to quantify trend impacts and the shift of impressions toward lower-monetizing regions, which the bull did not directly rebut. Neither side fully resolved the other's key concerns, so the debate is balanced.
